findings.headline: Wires are your most expensive line in the cohort.
findings.body: Outgoing international wires ($65 vs a $40 median, 89th percentile — above the $60 75th-percentile mark) and outgoing domestic wires ($25 vs $15, 83rd percentile) both price near the top of 9 and 12 peer banks respectively. Wire senders are typically businesses and higher-balance households — the customers you least want comparing schedules.

findings.stat_label: your NSF fee vs peer median
findings.headline: Your NSF fee is double the peer median.
findings.body: At $30.00, your returned-item fee is 2x the median of 34 comparable banks — the 82nd percentile. A quarter of the cohort now charges $6.25 or less as the industry retreats from NSF pricing under regulatory scrutiny. This is the most visible consumer line on your schedule.

findings.headline: Your two most-watched fees are missing from the data.
findings.body: Overdraft and monthly maintenance — the categories regulators and comparison sites watch most closely — did not appear in your published schedule data. Peers publish these lines (medians of $30 and $12); until you do, comparisons happen without your side of the story.

exec_narrative: Net position: Kentland Bank carries a consistent premium on the fees customers incur when money moves or goes wrong — international wires at the 89th percentile, domestic outgoing wires at the 83rd, NSF at double the peer median, and card replacement at twice the median — while core service lines like cashier's checks, incoming wires, and deposited-item returns price at or slightly below market. The exposure is concentrated: four lines account for essentially all of the above-market posture, and two of the most scrutinized categories are absent from the published data entirely. The three findings above are the agenda for a one-hour pricing conversation.

callouts.title: Outgoing wires — $65.00 international, $25.00 domestic
callouts.stat: Intl: peer median $40.00 · P75 $60.00 · 89th percentile · n=9 — Domestic: peer median $15.00 · 83rd percentile · n=12
callouts.body: Both outgoing wire fees sit at or near the top of the cohort, and the international fee clears the 75th percentile with room to spare. At $25 over the international median, this is the largest single dollar gap on your schedule — earned on exactly the customer segment (businesses, high-balance households) with the most alternatives and the most reason to shop.

callouts.title: NSF / returned item — $30.00
callouts.body: The peer distribution tells the story: the median has fallen to $15 and a quarter of comparable banks now charge $6.25 or less as institutions retire NSF fees ahead of regulatory and reputational pressure. A $30 NSF fee is increasingly conspicuous. Whether the right answer is a cut, a cap, or a documented rationale, this line deserves a decision rather than a default.

callouts.title: Card replacement — $20.00
callouts.body: Twice the peer median for a routine service event — usually triggered by loss or fraud, when the customer is already frustrated. It earns little revenue and generates outsized irritation; several peers charge $5, and one charges nothing.

callouts.title: Publish the missing lines — and claim the quiet wins
callouts.stat: Overdraft and monthly maintenance flagged as data gaps · Deposited item return $10 vs $12 median (P47) · Incoming wire $10 vs $12.50 (P50)
callouts.body: Two of the most-compared fee categories are absent from your published data, which means comparisons happen without you. Meanwhile the receiving-side fees you do publish sit at or below median and earn no credit. Publishing the gaps and marketing the below-market lines costs nothing and converts an information deficit into a transparency story.

context_narrative:
Two currents define the fee landscape your schedule competes in. First, the retreat from NSF: large banks have largely eliminated returned-item fees, and the pressure has migrated down-market — visible in your own cohort, where the NSF median ($15) is half your posted fee and a quarter of peers charge $6.25 or less. Second, published fee schedules have become marketing documents: public, scraped, and compared, which turns every outlier line into a small reputational bet and every unpublished line into an open question.

Mid-sized community banks occupy an exposed middle: large enough to be swept into fee surveys and comparison tools, without the brand gravity that lets the largest institutions charge premiums quietly. In that position, the highest-leverage moves are surgical, not across-the-board — bring the two or three top-decile lines back toward the pack, publish what is missing, and let the rest of the schedule, which already prices at market, speak for itself.
